name: Kann
description: Gregory Gourdet's live-fire Haitian room is the one out-of-towners ask me about by name, and for once the hype checks out. Everything comes off the hearth, the dining room hums, and it walked away with the James Beard Best New Restaurant medal in 2023 plus a spot on the World's 50 Best Discovery list. Get a Resy the second the window opens.
must_try: Griyo, the twice-cooked pork shoulder off the fire

name: Le Pigeon
description: Gabriel Rucker's brick box on East Burnside has been quietly running this town's French conversation for years now, multiple Beard medals deep. Grab a seat at the chef's counter if you can stomach watching your dinner get built two feet away. It's a $140 tasting now, omnivore or vegetarian, no a la carte, no apologies.
must_try: The foie gras profiteroles

name: Coquine
description: Up on the shoulder of Mt. Tabor, Katy Millard's little farm-worshipping room is the kind of place regulars get territorial about. It made the 2025 James Beard Outstanding Restaurant finalist cut, the wine list is nerdy in the best way, and yes, you can get the famous salted chocolate chip cookies to go if the tasting menu isn't in the cards.
must_try: Roast duck with plum harissa, then the smoked-salt chocolate chip cookies

name: Nodoguro
description: Ryan Roadhouse moved his kaiseki temple downtown, and it's still the most serious sushi-adjacent seat in the city. Pick the 15-course sousaku track or, if you've cleared your evening, the 20-plus-course marathon. He's a 2026 Beard finalist for Best Chef: Northwest, and it shows in every knife stroke.
must_try: Dungeness crab custard on the sousaku tasting

name: Gado Gado
address: 1801 NE César E. Chávez Blvd, Portland, OR 97232
description: Thomas Pisha-Duffly cooks his Chinese-Indonesian heritage loud and generous up in Hollywood, and the room feels like a good party you got invited to by accident. He's a 2026 James Beard Best Chef: Northwest finalist, so book ahead of the crowd that news brought in.
must_try: Scallop crudo with pandan cream

name: Han Oak
description: Peter Cho runs an ever-changing preset menu of Korean cooking built on Oregon ingredients out of what's basically his family's courtyard in Kerns. Noodle and dumpling nights, the occasional karaoke, kids underfoot. It's minimalist and chic but it eats like somebody's home, which is the whole point.
must_try: Coke-braised galbi-jjim short ribs

name: Kachka
description: Bonnie Morales turned the food of the former Soviet republics into one of Portland's great nights out. The infused vodka flight is not optional in my book, and the zakuski spread keeps landing until you cry uncle. Loud, warm, and a little chaotic in exactly the right way.
must_try: Siberian pelmeni dumplings with a horseradish vodka

name: Langbaan
description: A hidden tasting-menu counter behind a Northwest Thai restaurant, digging into historical and regional recipes most menus never touch. Seats are limited, the charcoal grill does serious work, and reservations vanish fast. This is culture-class Thai cooking, not your weeknight pad see ew.
must_try: The seasonal charcoal-grilled course on the tasting menu

name: Ox
address: 2225 NE Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd, Portland, OR 97212
description: Wood-grilled Argentine-style cooking on lower MLK, and the smoke gets into everything in the best possible way. The clam and bone marrow chowder is the dish people write home about, but the wood-grilled meats are the reason to come hungry. Expect a wait; it's earned.
must_try: Smoked bone marrow clam chowder

name: Eem
description: The mashup nobody knew they needed: Thai curries meet Texas-style smoked brisket on North Williams, with a cocktail program that punches well above the room. Come early or come patient, and get a frozen drink into your hand while you wait. Pure Portland in one plate.
must_try: Burnt-ends brisket coconut curry

name: República
description: Nixtamal from scratch, complex moles, and an ambitious Mexican tasting approach in the Pearl. This is the fine-dining end of Portland's Mexican cooking, corn milled and pressed in-house, and it reads on the plate. Reserve and give yourself the evening.
must_try: The house mole with fresh nixtamalized-corn tortillas

name: Higgins Restaurant & Bar
description: Greg Higgins was doing farm-to-table downtown before the phrase got tired, and this James Beard-winning stalwart near the Schnitzer is still the grown-up room in town. The bar side does one of the great pastrami sandwiches in the city if the white tablecloth isn't your speed tonight.
must_try: Grass-fed beef brisket pastrami sandwich at the bar

name: Jacqueline
description: A little seafood room on Clinton that treats oysters and crudo with the respect they deserve. Hamachi, a proper raw bar, and a Maine lobster bun that regulars order on autopilot. Cozy enough to feel like a secret, good enough that it isn't one anymore.
must_try: Maine lobster bun

name: Screen Door Eastside
description: The line down East Burnside on a Sunday is a Portland institution, and no, there's no skipping it. Southern comfort brunch done at scale without losing the plot. Put your name in, walk get a coffee, and come back for the plate everybody's here for.
must_try: Fried chicken and waffles

name: Navarre
description: A chalkboard-menu wine bar on 28th that's been quietly excellent for two decades, ordering by checklist card, small European-Northwest plates, minimal fuss. The brunch does eggs about ten different ways. It's the neighborhood spot every neighborhood wishes it had.
must_try: Eggs done ten ways at brunch, plus whatever's chalked up that morning

name: St. Jack
description: Classic Lyonnaise bistro on the NW 23rd strip, doing the greatest hits properly: gougeres, steak frites, oxtail bourguignon. When somebody wants French without the tasting-menu commitment, this is where I point them. Cozy, dependable, and genuinely romantic on a rainy night.
must_try: Steak frites

name: Cartopia
address: SE 12th Ave & SE Hawthorne Blvd, Portland, OR 97214
description: This is the one that started the whole late-night pod religion back in 2008, and it still runs the corner of 12th and Hawthorne like it owns it. Roughly eight carts under string lights and a tent, most of them slinging until 3am on weekends. Come at midnight, order across three different carts, eat standing up in the rain like a local who's stopped noticing the rain.
must_try: Poutine from Potato Champion, hand-cut fries under gravy and cheese curds at an hour when you shouldn't
seasonal: Covered and heated, so it's a legitimate rainy-night play year-round; liveliest after 10pm

name: Hawthorne Asylum
description: Twenty-plus carts, indoor and covered seating, a bar, and enough range that a table of picky friends can each get exactly what they want and still eat together. This is where I send people who say 'I don't get the food cart thing' — an hour here fixes them. Vegan Southern, Thai, sushi, all in one lot.
must_try: Dirty Lettuce's vegan Southern comfort plates — nobody believes it's vegan until they're two bites in
seasonal: Well-covered, one of the more comfortable pods to hit in a downpour

name: Prost Marketplace
description: The walkable Mississippi Avenue pod, anchored by the German beer hall Prost next door — grab a liter, wander the carts, sit in the shared beer garden. It's the civilized way to do carts: a proper pint in hand while you decide between barbecue, vegan bowls, and gluten-free Indian.
must_try: Native Bowl's vegan rice bowls, then a beer at Prost to wash it down
seasonal: Beer garden shines on a dry summer evening; Mississippi's at its best June through September

name: The Heist
description: Woodstock's pod with the thing every Portlander secretly wants in winter: real indoor seating, covered outdoor tables, and a proper bar. Korean fried chicken, bulgogi, Guyanese bake — heavy hitters in one lot on the quieter southeast side. This is my cold-and-wet-February pod.
must_try: Frybaby's Korean fried chicken, then a Kim Jong Grillin bibim box if you've still got room
seasonal: Indoor seating makes it a top rainy-day option; low-key year-round

name: Matt's BBQ
description: Texas-style brisket out of a food cart behind Prost on Mississippi, and yes, it's as good as the line suggests. Matt Vicedomini's been running the offset smoker on oak since 2015, moving 800-plus pounds of brisket a week. Go early — they cook it daily and sell out, and 'sold out' is not a suggestion here.
must_try: The fatty brisket, sliced to order, with pickles and the warm dip sauce
seasonal: Get there before 1pm on summer weekends or the brisket's a memory

name: Nong's Khao Man Gai
address: 609 SE Ankeny St, Ste C, Portland, OR 97214
description: Nong Poonsukwattana started with one cart and one dish in 2009 and basically taught the whole city what khao man gai is. Poached chicken, rice cooked in the broth, and that sauce — fermented soybean, ginger, garlic, chili — that people buy by the bottle. It grew into brick-and-mortar but it's the same laser-focused plate. This is Portland cart-scene history you can eat.
must_try: Khao man gai — poached chicken over broth-cooked rice, and do not skip the sauce

name: Kim Jong Grillin'
description: Han Ly Hwang's Korean cart, going since 2009 and now parked at The Heist in Woodstock. Bold, unfussy, generous — bibim boxes, kimchi fried rice, short rib. Another one of those carts that could've gone full restaurant years ago and just... didn't need to. The cart is the point.
must_try: The KJG bibim box — grilled meat, vegetables, egg, and rice built to order

name: Stumptown Coffee Roasters (Division Street)
description: The original. Opened on Division in 1999 in an old beauty parlor called Hair Bender — which is why the flagship espresso blend carries that name and the sign still hangs inside. Stumptown wrote the third-wave playbook everyone else photocopied: direct trade, obsessive sourcing, baristas treated like craft. Order a Hair Bender espresso at the flagship counter and you're drinking Portland coffee history.
must_try: A Hair Bender espresso, pulled at the cafe where the blend was born

name: Coava Coffee Roasters
address: 1300 SE Grand Ave, Unit A, Portland, OR 97214
description: The roaster the locals are quietly loyal to — Coava's beans turn up in good cafes all over town, but the SE Grand roastery-cafe is where you drink it at the source. Airy, bamboo-and-concrete room, single-origin obsession, pour-overs done with the seriousness of a chemistry lab. If Stumptown is the famous one, Coava is the one your barista friend actually brews at home.
must_try: A single-origin pour-over — ask what just came off the roaster

name: Breakside Brewery (Dekum Pub)
description: The Woodlawn flagship brewpub for one of Oregon's most decorated breweries — Breakside has taken Brewery of the Year at the Oregon Beer Awards repeatedly, including 2026. Hop-forward is the house language, and the Breakside IPA is the one you'll see in every Portland fridge. Industrial-style room with a patio, full bar, dog-friendly, all-ages — a proper neighborhood pub with serious beer behind the taps.
must_try: The Breakside IPA, on tap at the source
seasonal: Patio's the play on a dry summer evening; cozy indoors when it's pouring

name: Scotch Lodge
description: Down a flight of stairs into what feels like a warm cellar, this is where I take out-of-towners who think Portland can't do polished. Hundreds of whiskies behind the bar and a cocktail program that takes it all seriously without making you feel underdressed. Bring your reading glasses for the list.
must_try: The Peated & Confused, or just let the bartender walk you through a Scotch flight

name: Rum Club
description: Serving well-made rum-forward drinks since 2011, and it hasn't lost a step. Snug, unpretentious, and the kind of place where the daiquiri comes out exactly right every single time. The regulars order the Rum Club Daiquiri and don't overthink it. Neither should you.
must_try: The Rum Club Daiquiri

name: Hey Love
description: Attached to the Jupiter NEXT hotel, this jungle-plant-filled room is where the city goes to pretend it isn't raining sideways outside. Tropical drinks, a good slushie when the sun does show up, and a crowd that skews younger and louder as the night goes.
must_try: A frozen slushie cocktail on the patio during a rare dry evening
seasonal: Patio and slushies shine in the dry summer months

name: Angel Face
description: No printed cocktail menu here on purpose. You tell the bartender your spirit and your mood, and they build you something on the spot. It's a small French-leaning jewel box on 28th's restaurant row, and the whole trust-fall is the point. Come hungry too, the food is real.
must_try: A bartender's-choice cocktail built around your preferred spirit

name: Palomar
description: A bright, loud ode to Havana that packed up its old Division Street room and reopened on NW 23rd in spring of 2025. Cuban cooking, daiquiris that mean business, and a bartender-owner who talks rum like a professor. This is the one I send friends to when they want fun over hushed reverence.
must_try: The Floridita Daiquiri

name: Wayfinder Beer
description: Big industrial room under the bridges where Portland's lager renaissance basically lives. This is the birthplace of the Cold IPA, and brewmaster Kevin Davey's crisp, dry pours drink beautifully with the smoke-kissed pub food. When someone insists all Portland beer is hazy juice, I bring them here.
must_try: A Cold IPA, the style they helped define

name: Breakside Brewery
description: The original Dekum pub in Woodlawn, where the medal-hauling IPAs started. Great American Beer Festival gold, a wall of World Beer Cup hardware, and still a neighborhood corner pub at heart. Order the flagship IPA on a patio afternoon and understand why the trophy case is so crowded.
must_try: The Breakside IPA

name: The Sandy Hut
description: Open since 1923 and known to the faithful as the Handy Slut. Wood paneling, oddball vintage celebrity paintings, a back patio, and stiff well drinks poured by bartenders who actually like you. This is the friendly, welcoming end of the Portland dive spectrum. Cash in your pocket doesn't hurt.
must_try: A strong well whiskey and a seat under the weird celebrity portraits

name: The Yamhill Pub
description: Here since 1934 and gloriously unbothered by the century happening around it. This is downtown's diviest dive, a place that once moved more Pabst than anywhere in the country and has the plaques to prove it. Cheap beer, real characters, zero pretense. Come for the history, stay because your dollar goes far.
must_try: A can of PBR, as tradition demands

name: Heart Coffee Roasters
description: The bright, white-tiled Burnside flagship that put Portland light-roast on the map back in 2009. Single-origins from Kenya, Ethiopia, and Latin America, pulled with Scandinavian precision. If you take your coffee black and take it seriously, this is the counter seat to claim.
must_try: A single-origin espresso or a filter pour-over of the current Ethiopian

name: Push x Pull
description: A small Stark Street roaster the coffee nerds guard a little jealously. They chase fruit-forward naturals and honey-process lots that taste more like a bowl of berries than a cup of coffee. If you think you don't like light roast, let them change your mind on a slow morning.
must_try: A fruit-forward natural-process pour-over

name: Water Avenue Coffee
description: Tucked in the Central Eastside industrial district, this is the roaster for people who want a proper, comforting cup without a lecture. Direct-trade sourcing, dependable espresso, and a warehouse-adjacent room that fills with regulars on their way to work. Solid, unfussy, consistent.
must_try: A cappuccino made with their house espresso blend

name: Nossa Familia Coffee
description: Started in 2004 out of a family's own Brazilian coffee farms and grew into Oregon's first certified B Corp roaster. The Pearl District cafe is bright and welcoming, the sourcing story is genuinely direct-trade, and the espresso is dialed. Feel-good coffee that also happens to taste good.
must_try: An espresso made with their Brazilian family-farm beans

name: Never Coffee
address: 4243 SE Belmont St Ste 200, Portland, OR 97215
description: Minimal monochrome cafe where the signature lattes go delightfully off-script. The Midnight Oil leans on licorice syrup and the Oregon latte hides hops and dulce de leche. Not the spot for purists, but if you want coffee that plays, the Belmont room is a treat.
must_try: The Midnight Oil latte with licorice syrup

name: Ken's Artisan Bakery
description: Ken Forkish's Northwest Portland institution, and yes, that's the same Ken who wrote the book on flour, water, salt, and yeast. Organic country loaves, laminated pastry that shatters correctly, and morning lines that move because everyone knows exactly what they want. Get there before the good stuff runs.
must_try: The seasonal Oregon berry croissant with hazelnut cream
seasonal: Berry pastries peak in summer fruit season

name: Little T American Baker
description: The Division Street corner bakery locals folded into their weekly routine long ago and Travel + Leisure eventually caught onto. Excellent bread, honest pastries, and a light lunch counter that makes it a real morning-to-midday stop. Grab a loaf on the way out; you'll regret it if you don't.
must_try: A fresh-baked loaf or the morning pastry of the day

name: Portland Art Museum
description: The Pacific Northwest's oldest art museum, and after the long Rothko Pavilion build-out it finally connects its two buildings without you dodging traffic on the sidewalk. Native American and Asian galleries anchor a collection that punches above a city this size. I duck in on a gray afternoon and pretend I understand the Rothko.
must_try: Standing with the Monet 'Water Lilies' canvas in the European galleries

name: Oregon Museum of Science and Industry (OMSI)
description: Six acres of hands-on science on the east bank of the Willamette, with a planetarium, a real submarine tied up out front, and enough buttons to occupy a kid for a full rainy Saturday. Last Wednesday of the month it goes 21+ for OMSI After Dark, which is science class with a beer in your hand.
must_try: Touring the USS Blueback submarine docked in the river

name: Lan Su Chinese Garden
description: A full walled Ming-dynasty scholar's garden dropped into a single Old Town block, hand-built by Suzhou artisans. Come through the moon gate and the traffic noise just stops. This is where the Pods & Portals story really starts, right at the heart of the neighborhood that fed Portland's immigrant cooking.
must_try: Tea in the Tower of Cosmic Reflections teahouse over Lake Zither

name: Portland Japanese Garden
description: Up in the Washington Park hills, eight garden styles arranged with a precision that makes my apartment feel like a crime scene. Widely called the most authentic Japanese garden outside Japan. Locals know the secret: come when it's drizzling and half-empty, the moss glows, and you get the maples nearly to yourself.
must_try: The raked Flat Garden view from the Cultural Village veranda
seasonal: Peak in fall for maple color and spring for blossoms

name: Pittock Mansion
description: A 1914 French Renaissance chateau the city rescued from the wrecking ball in 1964, built by the newspaper man who founded The Oregonian. Tour the period rooms, but the real draw is the east lawn: on a clear day the whole city lines up under Mount Hood like a postcard nobody had to Photoshop.
must_try: The downtown-and-Mount-Hood panorama from the east lawn
hours: Daily 10am-4pm (Tue opens noon); seasonal and holiday closures
seasonal: Closed for maintenance part of January

name: Portland Chinatown Museum
description: A small, sharp museum in the bones of Old Town Chinatown telling the story most walking tours skip: the Chinese immigrant community that helped build this city and the neighborhood it made. Pair it with Lan Su a block away and you've got the whole Pods & Portals throughline before you ever taste a dumpling.
must_try: The 'Beyond the Gate' permanent exhibit on Portland's Chinatown history

name: Oregon Historical Society Museum
description: Across the South Park Blocks from the art museum, this is the state's memory bank: Oregon Trail artifacts, the messy real history, and the eight-story trompe-l'oeil murals on the outside wall that fool tourists every single day. Free for Multnomah County residents, which is the kind of civic detail a Regular appreciates.
must_try: The 'Experience Oregon' permanent exhibition

name: Oregon Zoo
description: Up in Washington Park and reachable by MAX light rail, which is the move on a summer day when parking turns feral. Known for its elephants and its Pacific Northwest habitats, plus summer concerts on the lawn. Bring a rain shell year-round; the animals are used to the weather and so should you be.
must_try: The Elephant Lands habitat
seasonal: Summer concert series on the lawn; ZooLights in winter

name: Portland Saturday Market
description: The largest continuously operating outdoor arts-and-crafts market in the country, running weekends under the Burnside Bridge in Old Town since 1974. Everything is made by the person selling it, which keeps it honest. Free to wander, and a straight shot from Lan Su and the Chinatown museum on the Pods & Portals loop.
must_try: An Elephant Ear fried-dough while browsing the maker booths riverside
seasonal: Open March through December only

name: Crystal Ballroom
description: A 1914 dance hall with a genuinely bouncing floating floor, mounted on ball-bearing rockers so the whole room moves when the crowd does. It has hosted everyone from James Brown to the current indie bill. First time you feel the floor ripple under a packed show you'll think you're dizzy. You're not. That's just the building.
must_try: Dancing on the mechanical floating ballroom floor at a sold-out show

name: Moda Center
address: 1 N Center Court St, Portland, OR 97227
description: The biggest arena in Oregon and home of the NBA's Trail Blazers over in the Rose Quarter, a short MAX hop across the river. It's the loud, communal heart of Portland sports even as the city argues about renovating it. Catch a Blazers night when the fast break gets rolling and 19,000 people lose their minds at once.
must_try: A Trail Blazers game with the Rose Quarter crowd on a fast break
seasonal: NBA season runs fall through spring

name: Providence Park
description: A century-old stadium wedged into the downtown grid, home to the MLS Timbers and NWSL Thorns and one of the most fervent supporter cultures in American soccer. The Timbers Army in the north end sings for ninety straight minutes. When Portland scores, Timber Joey fires up a chainsaw and cuts a slab off a log. It makes sense once you're there.
must_try: Standing in the Timbers Army north end for the log-slab goal celebration
seasonal: MLS and NWSL seasons run spring through fall

name: Helium Comedy Club
description: Portland's serious stand-up room on the inner east side, pulling national headliners into an intimate space where you're never more than 60 feet from the mic. Full food and drink menu, so you can heckle responsibly. Weekend shows sell out; the Portland's Funniest heats are worth catching before someone's famous.
must_try: A weekend headliner set from a table near the stage

name: Aladdin Theater
description: A restored 1927 movie house in Brooklyn-neighborhood southeast, now a 600-seat listening room with the kind of acoustics that reward a singer-songwriter and a hushed crowd. Seated, respectful, no talking through the quiet songs. It's where you go when you actually want to hear the show, not the guy behind you.
must_try: A seated singer-songwriter show in the restored 1927 house

name: Roseland Theater
description: A two-level Old Town standby that has been feeding Portland general-admission rock, hip-hop, and metal for decades, from small local bills to touring names. No frills, good sightlines, sticky floors that have earned it. Right in the Pods & Portals corridor if you want a show after your Chinatown wander.
must_try: A general-admission floor show at the Old Town mainstay

name: Revolution Hall
description: The old Washington High School auditorium in Buckman, reborn as one of the city's best-sounding mid-size rooms, seated or standing depending on the act. Come early for a drink on Martha's, the rooftop bar with a downtown view. It's a short walk off Hawthorne, so you can make a whole east-side night of it.
must_try: A show in the old high-school auditorium, then a drink on the rooftop Martha's bar

name: Forest Park & the Wildwood Trail
address: Lower Macleay trailhead, NW 29th Ave & Upshur St, Portland, OR 97210
description: Five thousand-plus acres of second-growth Doug fir stacked against the West Hills, and the 30-mile Wildwood Trail threading the whole length of it. This is the one I send everyone to first: you can be on a counter stool with a cortado downtown and, twenty minutes later, be alone in the ferns listening to a Swainson's thrush. Park free at Lower Macleay, walk up the creek to the Stone House ruin, and keep climbing to Pittock Mansion if your legs are honest about it.
must_try: The Lower Macleay to Pittock Mansion climb via the Wildwood Trail for the downtown-and-Mount-Hood payoff
seasonal: Best in the dry May-October window; trails get greasy and root-slick after PNW rains, so wear tread. Free summer Express Shuttle serves trailheads.

name: Hoyt Arboretum
description: Portland's museum of living trees: 2,300-some species spread over 12 miles of trail up in Washington Park. Locals treat it as the civilized way into the Wildwood system, redwoods and monkey puzzles and a Winter Garden that actually earns its name in January. The trails are free; only the parking meters have opinions. Grab a map at the visitor center and let the Overlook or Redwood loops set the pace.
must_try: The Redwood Trail through the towering coast redwood grove, then the Garden Connector down to the Rose Garden
seasonal: Year-round, but the conifer collection makes it one of the rare gardens worth walking in the grey months.

name: Mount Tabor Park
address: SE 60th Ave & Salmon St, Portland, OR 97215
description: One of only a handful of American cities with an extinct volcano inside the line, and ours is a 636-foot cinder cone on the east side turned into a 176-acre park. It's where the Southeast comes to jog, walk the reservoirs, and pretend the Wednesday car-free road closure is a spiritual practice. Clear evenings from the summit you get downtown, the West Hills, and Mount Hood lined up like a postcard nobody staged.
must_try: Sunset from the summit viewpoint above the historic open reservoirs
seasonal: Open year-round. Note: the picnic shelter and two nearby paths are closed May-August 2026 for a rebuild; the rest of the park stays open.

name: Sauvie Island Wildlife Area
address: 18330 NW Sauvie Island Rd, Portland, OR 97231
description: A Manhattan-sized river island fifteen minutes north where Portland goes to remember it lives on a floodplain. Flat, easy trails like the Wapato Greenway loop, sandy Willamette beaches for a summer float, and a birding scene that turns serious every fall when the sandhill cranes and geese pour in. The beaches want a $10 parking permit on summer weekends, and the far end rewards a long walk with Warrior Rock Lighthouse, Oregon's smallest.
must_try: The hike out to Warrior Rock Lighthouse, or fall raptor-and-crane birding from the Oak Island loop
hours: Daylight hours; check seasonal hunting-season access
seasonal: Beaches and swimming are a summer thing (permit required weekends); birding peaks in fall and winter. Parts of the wildlife area close for waterfowl hunting seasons.

name: Topaz Farm (formerly Kruger's Farm)
address: 17100 NW Sauvie Island Rd, Portland, OR 97231
description: If you grew up here you spent a few October afternoons at Kruger's; it sold, it's Topaz now, and honestly the experience survived the name change intact. Working farm on Sauvie, twelve miles out: U-pick fields, a big corn maze, farm stand, live-music nights in summer, and the fall harvest circus with the petting barn. It's the family-outing default for a reason, even if the reason is mostly cider donuts.
must_try: U-pick flowers and berries in summer; the corn maze and pumpkin fields at the Fall Harvest Festival
hours: Seasonal; roughly June through early November, daily in season
seasonal: June-early November operation. Berries and flowers in summer, pumpkins and corn maze through fall harvest; closed the deep winter.

name: Multnomah Falls
address: 53000 E Historic Columbia River Hwy, Bridal Veil, OR 97010
description: The 620-foot two-tiered showstopper in the Columbia Gorge, 45 minutes east and worth every one of the tour buses it draws. Walk the paved switchbacks up to Benson Bridge for the classic shot, then keep climbing to the top viewpoint if you want to earn the crowd-free part. Yes it's the postcard, but standing in the mist plume on a hot July afternoon reminds you why the postcard exists.
must_try: The 1.2-mile paved climb from Benson Bridge to the top-of-falls viewpoint
hours: Daylight; lodge and visitor center hours vary
seasonal: A $2 timed-use parking permit is required 9am-6pm daily, May 22-Sep 7, 2026 (book at Recreation.gov; it doesn't guarantee a spot). No permit needed if you bike, transit, or hike in, or visit off-season.

name: eNRG Kayaking
description: Straight talk: Portland Kayak Company retired and closed, so the easiest on-water option near town is now eNRG, sitting on a floating dock a mile below Willamette Falls in Oregon City. You walk off the rental counter straight onto the boat. Kayaks, SUPs, and canoes for self-guided paddles, plus guided tours up to the falls and the historic locks. They also run the Upper Clackamas whitewater in season.
must_try: The guided paddle up to the base of Willamette Falls and the historic locks
hours: Daily in season; seasonal hours vary
seasonal: Flatwater rentals and tours run the warm months; Upper Clackamas rafting trips run roughly April through Labor Day depending on flows.

name: Triangle Wine Country Tours
address: Hotel pickup in Portland; tours run the Willamette Valley, OR
description: The Willamette Valley is the whole reason people put up with Oregon Pinot prices, and the civilized way to do it is to let someone else drive. This woman-owned outfit runs small-group seven-hour tours with a certified wine pro, three wineries, lunch and snacks included, pickup from your Portland hotel. You get the vineyard views, the inside baseball on who's making what, and no argument about who's the designated driver.
must_try: A small-group Pinot Noir flight tour through the Dundee Hills with lunch included
seasonal: Runs year-round; summer and fall harvest are the peak season and book up. Reservations required.

name: Kerr Bikes (Wheel Fun Rentals) at Waterfront Park
description: Right on Tom McCall Waterfront Park, this is the grab-a-bike-and-go spot for the car-free riverfront loop. Standard bikes, e-bikes, tandems, and the goofy four-wheeled surreys if you're traveling with kids who won't pedal. The nice part: Kerr Bikes proceeds benefit Albertina Kerr, a local nonprofit for kids and adults with developmental disabilities, so the tourist surrey money does some good.
must_try: Renting a bike for the flat car-free loop along the Willamette across the Tilikum Crossing and back
seasonal: Busiest and most reliably open spring through fall; winter hours are limited and weather-dependent.

name: Portland Aerial Tram
description: Technically it's OHSU's commuter tram, but for the price of a general-admission ticket you get a three-minute climb from the South Waterfront up to Marquam Hill with the whole city, the river, and on a clear day Mount Hood and Mount St. Helens hanging in the window. It's the cheapest big view in town and the anchor of the local 4T loop (trail, tram, trolley, train) if you want to make a day of it.
must_try: A round trip at dusk for the Willamette-and-volcanoes panorama from the upper terminal
hours: Mon-Fri 5:30am-9:30pm, Sat 9am-5pm; closed Sundays (until May) and major holidays
seasonal: Runs year-round; clearest mountain views come on dry-season afternoons. Closed on Independence Day, Memorial Day, and Labor Day.

name: Tryon Creek State Natural Area
description: The only Oregon state park inside a major city, tucked in the ravine between Southwest Portland and Lake Oswego. Miles of soft trail through second-growth forest, eight bridges and a wetland boardwalk, and a nature center that runs a free family walk every Saturday morning. It's quieter and flatter than Forest Park, which makes it the pick when you want trees without a thigh workout. Trillium carpet the ground in early spring.
must_try: The Trillium Trail loop in March when the namesake wildflowers bloom
hours: Park dawn-dusk; nature center hours vary
seasonal: Year-round, muddy in the wet months (boardwalks help). Early-spring trillium bloom is the marquee event; free guided family walks Saturdays 10-11am.

name: Powell Butte Nature Park
description: An extinct cinder cone on the far east side, 600-plus acres of wildflower meadow and forest with the best in-city look at Mount Hood. The paved Mountain View Trail climbs gently to a summit with a 'Mountain Finder' panel that names the Cascade peaks lined up in front of you, and the wilder Wild Horse loops keep the mountain bikers happy. Underrated because it's a hike from downtown, which is exactly why the meadows stay this open.
must_try: The Mountain View Trail to the summit 'Mountain Finder' with Mount Hood dead ahead
seasonal: Open year-round; the meadow wildflowers peak late spring into summer and the exposed summit is glorious on a clear dry-season day.

name: Springwater Corridor & Oaks Bottom Wildlife Refuge
address: Oaks Bottom trailhead, SE Milwaukie Ave & SE Mitchell St, Portland, OR 97202
description: A 21-mile paved rail-trail that runs from the east bank of the Willamette out to Boring, and the stretch that matters most cuts right through Oaks Bottom, Portland's first designated urban wildlife refuge. Bike or walk it and you'll pass beavers, river otters, herons, and the giant painted mural on the wastewater plant that everyone photographs. Flat, car-free, and the local go-to for a long ride that never leaves the city.
must_try: Biking the Springwater from the waterfront through Oaks Bottom to the Sellwood bluff
seasonal: Rideable year-round; bird activity in the wetland peaks in spring and fall migration. Bikes stay on the paved corridor, not the refuge dirt trails.

name: Oregon River Experiences (Clackamas River Rafting)
address: Upper Clackamas River put-in near Estacada, OR (about 45 min from Portland)
description: The Wild & Scenic Upper Clackamas is the closest real whitewater to town, a 45-minute drive east, and this outfitter has been running Oregon rivers for 35-plus years. Class II through III+ day trips depending on how much you want the cold water in your face, guides who know the lines, and the kind of scenery that makes you forget you're this close to a metro area. The most accessible splash-and-giggle-to-genuine-thrills river Portland has.
must_try: A guided Class III+ day trip on the Upper Clackamas during spring snowmelt
hours: By reservation; day trips in season
seasonal: Rafting season runs roughly April through Labor Day, flow-dependent; spring snowmelt brings the bigger, colder water. Reservations required.

name: Smith and Bybee Wetlands Natural Area
description: Two thousand acres of freshwater wetland wedged between the Columbia Slough and the river out in North Portland, one of the largest urban wetlands in the country and one nobody expects to find behind the port terminals. Paddle a canoe or kayak among the lakes in the high-water months and you're sharing the place with beavers, river otters, painted turtles, osprey, and bald eagles. The paved interpretive trail handles the dry season when the lakes drop.
must_try: A winter-to-spring canoe paddle across the lakes when water levels are up
seasonal: Paddling window is roughly December through May when water levels are high; summer draws the lakes down to mudflats, so switch to the interpretive trail and boardwalk. Free parking, no fee.

name: Ecola State Park
address: 84318 Ecola Park Rd, Cannon Beach, OR 97110
description: The big-day side trip, about 90 minutes west at Cannon Beach, and the single best headland view on the north coast. Paved paths at Ecola Point put Haystack Rock, the offshore Tillamook Rock Lighthouse, and miles of coastline in one frame; the Clatsop Loop and Tillamook Head trails follow the ground Lewis and Clark walked. Come for the viewpoint, stay for the tide pools at Indian Beach, and time it for the gray whale migration if you can.
must_try: The Clatsop Loop hike to the Tillamook Head viewpoint over 'Terrible Tilly' lighthouse
seasonal: Open year-round; $10 day-use parking fee (or Oregon State Parks pass). Gray whale watching peaks in December-January and March-April; summer parking fills fast and lines form June-September.

name: Cartopia Food Carts
description: The one that started the late-night thing. Cartopia has anchored SE 12th and Hawthorne since 2008, and it's still where you end up at 11pm with a beer from the covered garden and a decision to make between poutine and a wood-fired pie. Fire pit's real, the regulars are real, and nobody's rushing you out.
must_try: Poutine from Potato Champion
seasonal: Covered seating and fire pit make it a genuine year-round rainy-day option, not just a summer pod

name: Prost! Marketplace
description: The pod on Mississippi that figured out the community-beer-garden model back in 2009, when the rest of the city was still treating carts as a lunch afterthought. Order a German bier from Prost proper, carry it into the marketplace, and let the carts sort out dinner. It's the blueprint half the newer pods are working from.
must_try: A liter of German bier from Prost paired with a smashburger from the pod
seasonal: Covered bier garden keeps it going through the wet months

name: Modhaus
description: The new kid on Division, opened just this year as a bar-and-cafe built around a cart pod. The lineup is doing the immigrant-foodways thing Portland does best: Makulit slinging Filipino mash-ups, Desi PDX's cardamom-chai fried chicken, Hawker Station's Cantonese, Chick & Pig on Thai. Bar's proper, so you can sit and settle in rather than eat-and-run.
must_try: Desi PDX's fried cardamom-chai chicken
seasonal: Indoor bar and cafe make it a comfortable cold-weather sit

name: WonderLove
description: The maximalist pod: three-story bar, live-music stages, public art, and a rooftop patio with a downtown skyline view that makes it feel more venue than parking lot. Opened in 2024 down at 2nd and Main. Come for the carts, stay because there's a band and a cocktail and you can't quite find the exit. During the World Cup they were showing USMNT matches on the turf.
must_try: A craft cocktail on the rooftop patio at golden hour with cart food in hand
seasonal: Rooftop shines in dry-season summer; indoor levels and covered tent carry the rain months

name: Lost Plate Food Tours
description: Small groups of four to ten, actual Portlanders as guides, and a three-hour walking route through the cart scene where the food and drinks are all folded into the price. They bill it as the city's only walking food-cart tour and back it up with owner stories you wouldn't get eating solo. There's also a wine-tasting version and a coffee-and-donut morning if carts aren't your speed.
must_try: The walking food cart tour; let the guide order the dishes tourists never find
seasonal: Runs year-round; book the covered-pod-heavy route in the rainy months

name: Forktown Food Tours
description: The elder statesman, running tours since 2010, which in Portland food-tour years is roughly forever. Three neighborhood routes to pick from: Downtown for the classics, Mississippi Avenue for the artsy east-side sprawl, and Division Street for the global-and-wine crawl. Small groups, two-ish hours, seven-ish stops, minimal walking, maximal eating.
must_try: The Division Street tour for its wine bar, micro cart pods, and Indian street snacks

name: Portland Food Cart Tours
description: Led by Brett Burmeister, the managing editor of FoodCartsPortland, which is about as close to a walking encyclopedia of the pod scene as you'll get. Ninety minutes, four carts, and a running narration on why the whole cart thing works here and nowhere else quite the same. This is the history-and-context tour for people who want to understand the pods, not just eat at them.
must_try: The downtown cart-history walk; you're paying for Brett's institutional memory as much as the food

name: City Brew Tours Portland
description: Used to be Brewvana, now flies the City Brew Tours flag, but the Portland team and routes stayed local, which is the part that matters. Flagship public tour hits three or four breweries with multiple pours at each, a gourmet snack break, and a guide who knows the brewers by name and steers the route by whatever's interesting in Portland beer that week. Van gets you between stops, so nobody's driving.
must_try: The flagship public brewery tour with the guided tasting flights

name: A Great Oregon Wine Tour
description: Full-day, small-group runs from Portland out into the Willamette Valley, three or four hand-picked vineyards, a picnic-style lunch, and door-to-door service so the pinot noir isn't a designated-driver problem. Every tour's custom and the guides lean educational, which suits both the wine nerd and the person who just learned Oregon does world-class pinot.
must_try: The full-day Willamette Valley pinot noir circuit with the wine-country picnic lunch
seasonal: Valley is gorgeous late summer through fall harvest; tastings run year-round

name: Sea to Summit Tours & Adventures
description: Portland guides who've been at this since 2001 and will happily bury you in geology and history between stops. The menu is deep: Willamette Valley wine, the Columbia River Gorge and Multnomah Falls, a Hood River wine run, brewery tours. Book direct and it's usually cheaper than the third-party platforms, which is the kind of tip a regular passes along.
must_try: The Columbia Gorge and Multnomah Falls tour with the roadside geology lesson
seasonal: Gorge waterfalls run hardest in spring snowmelt; summer is prime dry-season touring

name: Wildwood Adventures
description: Small-group half- and full-day trips in late-model vans with the big panoramic windows, which sounds like a small thing until you're watching Multnomah Falls slide past in the rain. They do the Mt. Hood and Columbia Gorge waterfall loop with a stop at the 1925 Multnomah Falls Lodge, plus Willamette Valley wine tastings. Downtown pickup, no logistics on you.
must_try: The Columbia Gorge waterfalls tour with the stop at the historic Multnomah Falls Lodge
seasonal: Waterfalls thunder in spring; wineries best in fall harvest

name: Waterfall Shuttle
address: Director Park, 815 SW Park Ave, Portland, OR 97205
description: Founded in 2020 to solve the very Portland problem of Multnomah Falls being gorgeous and impossible to park at. Runs seven days a week, morning, noon, and night, from Director Park downtown, hitting five big Gorge waterfalls with short walks at each for the photo. Wheelchair-accessible, hotel pickups, and it quietly moved 20,000 people its first year for a reason.
must_try: The half-day five-waterfall Gorge run, or the sunset tour for the light
seasonal: Spring snowmelt is peak waterfall volume; year-round operation

name: The Society Hotel
description: A boutique-hostel hybrid in a restored 1881 building right in Old Town Chinatown, which puts you a short walk from Lan Su Chinese Garden and the whole Pods-and-Portals corridor. Bunk-room beds if you're counting dollars, private rooms if you're not, and a rooftop deck for the skyline. The best base in the city for eating your way through the immigrant foodways downtown.
must_try: A morning coffee on the rooftop deck before walking to Lan Su Chinese Garden

name: The Nines, a Luxury Collection Hotel
description: The grande dame, stacked into the top floors of the historic Meier & Frank building steps from Pioneer Square and Powell's. Two restaurants worth the elevator ride: Departure for modern Asian with a downtown view, and Urban Farmer for a local-sourced steakhouse take. If you want to sleep above the culinary action rather than beside it, check rates here.
must_try: Dinner at Departure for the modern Asian menu and the skyline view

name: Kimpton Hotel Vintage Portland
description: A wine-themed Kimpton in the heart of downtown, rooms named for local wineries and a complimentary evening wine hour that's basically a soft launch for your Willamette Valley tour the next morning. Bacchus Bar downstairs handles the craft cocktails. Well placed for Powell's, the Schnitzer, and a cart lunch, and it leans romantic without trying too hard.
must_try: The complimentary evening wine hour pouring Oregon labels

name: Powell's City of Books
description: The one everybody means when they say they're going to Powell's. A full city block, new and used shelved side by side, color-coded rooms so you can pretend you won't get lost (you will). I still tell first-timers to start in the Blue Room and just surrender the afternoon.
must_try: Climbing to the third-floor Rare Book Room, then finding a used copy shelved next to the new one downstairs

name: Music Millennium
description: The Pacific Northwest's oldest surviving record store, open since 1969, and yes, Terry's looking for a successor now that he's 70, so shop it while it's still Terry's. Best year they've ever had, which tells you vinyl in this town never actually died. Free in-store sets if you time it right.
must_try: Flipping the new-arrivals vinyl bins and catching a free in-store performance

name: Tender Loving Empire
description: Part gift shop, part record label, all Portland since 2007, stocking 700-odd small makers. The downtown flagship a block off the transit mall is the one to hit. Where else does the jam sit next to a vinyl release from the store's own label.
must_try: A record from their in-house label tucked in beside the handmade jewelry and local jam

name: Portland Farmers Market at PSU
description: The flagship Saturday market, 150-plus vendors strung down the South Park Blocks under the elms, up to 13,000 people weekly. Year-round, rain or shine, which in this town is a promise and a warning. Come hungry and bring a tote.
must_try: Hood strawberries in June, chanterelles come fall
seasonal: Open Saturdays year-round; peak bounty June through October

name: Movie Madness
description: A nonprofit video store with 80,000-plus titles in a streaming world, which is exactly the kind of stubborn Portland only makes sense of. Now run by the Hollywood Theatre. The back room is a free props museum, and the VHS players come courtesy of Free Geek. Deep cuts, cult rarities, an LGBTQ section that puts the chains to shame.
must_try: The free film-props museum in back, home to the actual knife from Psycho's shower scene

name: Next Adventure
description: Three floors of hiking, camping, paddle and snow gear on Grand Ave, locally owned since 1997, and it nearly closed this year before the founders un-retired to keep it that way. The soul of the place is the Bargain Basement, where used gear goes to find a second summit. Skip REI, come here.
must_try: Digging through the Bargain Basement for used tents, boots, and paddles

name: Cargo
description: Twenty thousand square feet of restored brick warehouse in the Central Eastside, packed floor to rafters with direct-imported furniture, temple salvage, paper lanterns, tin toys, and party goods you didn't know you needed. Free parking out back, which in this district is its own small miracle. Budget more time than you think.
must_try: Getting happily lost among the paper lanterns, tin toys, and architectural salvage

name: Mississippi Records
description: Named for the street it left, which is the most Portland thing about it. Record store, label, repair shop, and cafe, with the tiny Portland Museum of Modern Art tucked in the basement. Heavy on rock and pop but real depth in jazz, soul, funk, and international. Open every day, noon to seven.
must_try: A Mississippi Records label reissue, then the PMOMA in the basement

name: Broadway Books
description: Locally owned indie on NE Broadway since 1992, heavy on literary fiction, history, and memoir. Small enough that the staff actually read what they shelve, and the handwritten picks prove it. Free gift wrap, happy to special-order, closed Mondays.
must_try: Whatever's talked up on the handwritten staff-picks shelf

name: Cycle Portland Bike Tours & Rentals
description: Old Town shop that'll get you rolling for eighteen bucks, lock, helmet, and route map included, no ceremony. Guided tours too, from the Essential loop through Old Town and the waterfront to a Brews Cruise you shouldn't schedule before anything important. Reserve ahead in summer.
must_try: The Essential Portland tour looping Old Town and the waterfront esplanade
seasonal: Open March 1 through December 23

name: Buffalo Exchange (Hawthorne)
description: The Hawthorne resale landmark, a block off the strip and steps from the Bagdad. Buy, sell, or trade a bag of your closet for cash or credit any day they're open, no appointment. The more current your taste, the better your odds at the counter. Comb the sale rack, everyone does.
must_try: Trading a bag from your closet for store credit, then working the clearance rack

name: Xtabay Vintage
description: Not thrift, curation. Since 2001 this Clinton Street boutique has dealt in pristine women's vintage from Edwardian through the mid-1980s, with the later racks tipping into designer and couture. The place people quietly come to for the one-of-a-kind wedding or prom dress. Weekends only, so plan for it.
must_try: Trying on a museum-grade Edwardian-to-1950s gown you'll find nowhere else

name: Beam & Anchor
description: A restored 7,000-square-foot warehouse where the retail floor sits under a working maker studio, which is about as Portland as a retail concept gets. Vintage and refurbished furniture, studio ceramics, organic fragrance, small-batch everything. Weekends and by appointment, so don't just wander up on a Tuesday expecting an open door.
must_try: A piece of hand-thrown pottery made in the studio upstairs

name: Pistils Nursery
description: The Mississippi District flagship, going on twenty-plus years of talking Portlanders into just one more houseplant. Tropicals, cacti, air plants, hand-thrown pots, and urban-farm supply, curated by people who clearly can't stop either. Dangerous on a slow Sunday.
must_try: An oddball rare houseplant paired with a hand-thrown pot to match

name: Everybody's Bike Rentals & Tours
description: The northside answer to a downtown rental shop, running refurbished vintage cruisers and modern bikes since 2012, a few pedal strokes from Alberta, Mississippi, and the Williams corridor. Each bike gets fitted to you and sent off with lights, lock, helmet, map, and a stack of local tips. This is how you do the arts districts.
must_try: Renting a refurbished vintage cruiser to roll the Alberta Arts District
